title: Zazen on the Road and in the Zendo
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Through their personal experience with zazen practice, Seiu Hannah Sullivan has come to understand that sitting with others in community can deepen our connection and understanding of ourselves and the world around us. By participating in group sittings, they've developed a sense of spaciousness and unity, even in challenging situations, and have found comfort in the unknown through repetition and silence. This experience has taught them the importance of compassion and mindfulness towards others, particularly in times of conflict and suffering, and has inspired them to cultivate non-separation, impermanence, and kindness.

sentences.text: When I think of sitting zazen, the wear of it moves almost anywhere.
Our last Shuso, Bob Rose, and I share a love of travel, and we've compared notes on how we manage a regular zazen practice in the far-flung places we find ourselves.
A couple of pillows crossed in a corner on a bed is something you'll find in nearly any place of lodging.
Unzip your travel bag, take out the ziplock holding your rakusu, do the robe chant, and you're on.
For many years, I held a solitary practice.

In yoga, the word was classes are great, but the real meat of the practice is in your daily home practice, so I followed that guideline for my home sitting practice and was quite comfortable doing it alone.
A significant change occurred when I hooked into the zazen community.
I suspect it was Norman Fischer who suggested that a very important aspect of our practice relied upon sitting with others, our sangha.

There is something that happens to me when I walk into a room that has been made into a zendo, like this one: the calming quality of black cushions against the wood of a polished floor, a set up that allows for silent entry, exit, kinhin, easy to follow, and a home.
My friend Dunia calls this your portable monastery.
I love visiting other sanghas and slipping into the quiet rhythm of sitting together.
There's a quality of friendship that can develop over the years without words.
I've bowed across the room to someone for days and have come to feel very close to them, despite knowing absolutely nothing about their life, their job, or their family.
As for what happens when the eyes lower to a gaze somewhere a few feet distant, it's one of those indescribable things that maybe shouldn't have words to constrain it.
It's very private, personal, yet it sends us into a place of vast unity.
During this practice period, I've had such a good time sharing the discovery of the Diamond Sutra.
For me, it was a very long path to even want to read such material.
I found myself thinking of each of you as I read and prepared for classes.
I was stunned and thrilled to hear some of the sharing that came across the Zoom screen and allusions to some talk from the breakout rooms.
Here we would be kicking around ideas that maybe even months earlier were stumbling blocks to me.
The wonderful discovery was that we weren't trying to find the perfect, correct answer, but more that we took a step into the unknown together and felt it out.
This is how I would characterize my experience in Zazen today: taking a step into the unknown without fear and just being there with it.

I think when I first sat using techniques including guided visualizations, sweeping the body for places that were holding or focusing on a specific word or thought, there was value, but it has been in the silence of Shikantaza, of just sitting, that I have been able to hold the various cries of the world.
Not to try to change them, although I must confess that I have had some absolutely excruciating sits.

Body aches and pains that were horrendous, experimenting with endless cushion combinations, wrestling with the idea of whether sitting on a chair was as good as sitting on a cushion, finding something that worked perfectly only to have that same position or combo become unworkable.
So you get your designated little space all fixed up, then comes the sitting practice.
This is going to sound like I know what I'm doing, but the fact is that you don't know what's going to happen when you sit on your cushion.
You might have a spectacularly empty, spacious experience, and you may be just counting the breaths or the moments to when that sit is going to be done.
My root teacher, Peter Levitt, gave a little example one day of being in a session and sitting and it just got so long and finally he couldn't stand it anymore.
He snuck a look at his watch and he had been sitting for seven minutes.
So you just don't know.
Through this practice period I have joined the 7 a.m. sitting group.
Years of shift work made me into a night owl who doesn't automatically awaken at 5 a.m., but what a lovely experience has arisen.
I smile into the zoom screen when I see my fellow practitioners.
Even when tired, I know if I can just roll out of bed and get myself to the cushion or even get up early enough to make a cup of coffee first, I will not regret it.
In the evening sitting for 40 minutes prior to Dharma seminar on the Diamond Sutra, I was ready for class.
I could leave anything that was going on out there in the world for a little while and find more room for contemplation, for discussion with like-minded friends and do it wholeheartedly.
So why the silence?
Zen is famous for silence, and I suppose I can't just limit it to Zen, but the silent retreat particularly.
The first time I went to a long retreat, the teacher was Mr.
S.
N.
Goenka, and he told a story, and I'm just gonna butcher his Burmese accent, but he said, "Why do we not talk?
You talk to your friend in between.

You say, 'Hey, what you got?' Your friend says, 'I got tingling.' You go, 'Oh, I want tingling too.'" Enough to just give ourselves the room to not be taking whatever we had, whatever that conversation was that we squeezed in back onto the cushion.
That vow of silence really changes our sitting.
I've gone from hoping something spacious would happen to not worrying about whether I was getting it and finding that I have a capacity for spaciousness.
This is not to say I have perfected the art of sitting zazen.
The surprise thoughts that enter the memory of some long forgotten experience.
Well, we talk about impermanence.
When Suzuki Roshi was dying, a couple of his students asked him to tell them the core of Buddhism.
The story goes that he was quiet and then said, "Everything changes.
We need look no further than our own homes for dealing with change."
Being a parent with small children is a constant changing circus.
Whether you live with a partner or live alone, something will happen that was not like this yesterday, and we get to live through it.
I think that zazen has opened me in a way that I can meet the changing face of reality with increasingly less drama and fear of the unknown.
If I can look into my body at the time of challenge and really feel it, really turn toward the feeling, the mental state, the nagging pain, I can pretty much ride through the change.
I read something yesterday describing Bodhisattvas as riding the waves of birth and death, and that feels really true to me.
Most of you know that in my own family, two major events happened during the practice period: my husband Jerry had open heart surgery and our son-in-law died.

To have the comfort of practice, the wide open landscape that could include absorbing the unknown of medical conditions or the daily details of healing that could open my heart to my daughter's grief over the loss of the love of her life has been sort of amazing, and I would like to thank my husband Jerry for telling me a couple days after his surgery.
I don't think you have to change much of anything about your involvement in this practice period.
You can take care of me at the same time.
Sitting zazen, then sitting again.
My wonderful teacher and friend Kathy Fisher has often spoken of the value of repetition in our practice.
This was especially helpful when sinking into the old language of the Diamond Sutra, joking sometimes in the breakout rooms, "Okay, we get it.
Can we just move on?"
Whether we got it or not, all that repetition.
But the repetition that works a sort of magic in difficult situations can happen over time.
I will use the example of my daughter's husband.
He struggled with alcohol for his entire adulthood.
As his disease developed and increased, I watched myself going through the usual worries parents have for their children, no matter how old these children might be.
The repetition of zazen worked on me as I sifted through this nemesis of a family member.
He blew all my perceptions of myself as an open-minded person.
He triggered huge portions of my life as the child of an alcoholic, the sister of a brother who died of alcohol, and perplexed me no end.
Along the line, I recognized that I no longer had to judge him or have expectations of him changing.
I can't say how or when it happened.
I just lost the wall between myself and him.
I saw something similar happen with a fellow sangha member some years ago.
Different storyline completely.
She just was simply driving me crazy.
One day, it occurred to me that I didn't have to feel that way any longer.
How can this be?
I credit it all to our practice.
As we studied the Diamond Sutra together, I became aware of how much we can push ourselves to get it.
And sometimes getting it is far beyond understanding.
Like a lock in a safe tumbling into the open position.
It's a feeling.
It's perhaps a phrase.
Like a flickering lamp, reads one translation of the last line of the Diamond Sutra.
I read a Gary Snyder poem at the beginning of practice period, a clean little observation of things in the wild.
And the last line is, "What do we know?"
Rather than a worry, I find that a comfort.
We don't have to be the kid in the class with their hand up all the time.
And in the evolution of Zoom gatherings, I've been introduced to the concept of stepping forward and stepping back.
Asking people when it's time to share to consider what their conditioned response usually is to that moment, and to do the other.
So an empty mind, one that does not necessarily know the answer, is a mind that might be able to find a new answer or make room for someone else's answer.
I think we desperately need this in our greater world today.
How can we understand others if we don't get out of the way and listen to those cries of the world?
I know all of us have been impacted by the world, by the war in Ukraine that is happening right now as we sit on our quiet cushions.
Many of us have expressed deep anxiety, and I am sure that many of us have children, in my case grandchildren, who are affected in ways that cause us great concern.
While the invasion of Ukraine continues, we grieve our ailing planet, suffer through heat domes and calving glaciers, get or isolate from or treat people with COVID.
It's a scary world out there.

I want to refer you to a letter that I received via email that was written earlier this week by Joan Halifax, one of the influential Zen teachers of our time, as she voices so beautifully what so many are feeling.

When there is an other, there is an Auschwitz, a cast of people we will not touch, a ravaged and raped woman, a clear cut forest, an abused and abandoned child, a man behind bars medicated out of his mind and heart, a rundown village of old women whose men have all died in a war, a young man from Russia with fear and hate in his eyes and a gun in his hand prowling down a street in Kiev.
She goes on, many of us have not allowed ourselves to look deeper than our personality and yet, and our opinions, to see and touch who we really are.

Yet Buddhists and contemplatives of many traditions have long been guided to go within, to discover not only the interconnectedness of all things, including the natural world, but also the peace that surpasses understanding, knowing, ideas, conceptions, and opinions.

The peace that is basic to all beings when they have come home to a state of non-alienation and also the peace that nourishes courageous and liberating action in the world, knowing that this peace is not complacent, nor is it restless.
Out of this wise peace arises compassionate action.
If we see that we are not separate from others, then we not only share their awakening, we also share their suffering.

This morning, as I write these words, I am not separate from the fear and courage of Ukrainians who are taking a stand in the streets of their cities, but I am also separate from the suffering of those who are attacking the Ukraine.
Thank you, Joan, for that.
What I have learned in this study time is a deeper understanding of non-separation.

Like Subhuti, who wept when he really heard the Buddhist teachings of the Prajnaparamita, we can take solace in the impermanence, the flickering lamp in this fleeting world as we pay attention and do what we can.
And I'll close with Agata by Robert Aitken: "When people talk about war, I vow with all beings to raise my voice in the chorus and speak of original peace."
So thank you very much, and thank you to the wonderful teachers who have influenced this talk and my life.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to be kind.
